### Systems physiology: Auditory Brainstem Responses (ABR), Distortion Product Otoacoustic Emissions (DPOAE) and extracellular recordings from SGNs

ABR, DPOAE and extracellular recordings from single SGNs were performed essentially as described before (Jing et al., 2013; Strenzke et al., 2016). ABR and DPOAE recordings were performed on 6-week-old mice. For extracellular recordings from individual SGNs, 6 to 10 week-old mice were anesthetized by i.p. injection of urethane (1.32 mg/kg), xylazine (5 mg/kg) and buprenorphine (0.1 mg/kg), a tracheostomy was performed and the mice were then placed in a stereotactic system. After partial removal of the occipital bone and cerebellum to expose the anteroventral cochlear nucleus (AVCN), a glass microelectrode was advanced through the posterior AVCN portion to reach the auditory nerve. Acoustic stimulation was provided by an open field Avisoft ScanSpeak Ultrasonic Speaker (Avisoft Bioacoustics, Germany), and ‘putative’ SGNs (auditory nerve fibers formed by the central SGN axons) were identified and distinguished from cochlear nucleus neurons based on their stereotactic position (>1.1 mm from the surface of the cochlear nucleus), spontaneous and noise-burst induced firing, peristimulus time histogram (PSTH), regularity of firing, and first spike latency. Recordings were performed using TDT system III hardware and an ELC-03XS amplifier (NPI Electronics, Germany), offline analysis using waveform-based spike detection using custom-written MATLAB software (Source code 1).

### Transmission electron microscopy

#### Conventional embedding

Conventional embedding of organs of Corti was essentially performed as described previously (Wong et al., 2014). In brief, here P21, 6 weeks and 8 months old mice were used. The apical turn of organs of Corti were dissected in phosphate-buffer saline (PBS) and fixed for 1 hr on ice with 4% paraformaldehyde and 0.5% glutaraldehyde in PBS (pH 7.4). After an additional fixation overnight on ice with 2% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 7.2), samples were washed in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer and placed in 1% osmium tetroxide (v/v in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer) on ice for 1 hr. Next, samples were washed twice in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer (10 min each, on ice) and further in distilled water and subsequently en bloc stained with 1% uranyl acetate (v/v in distilled water) for 1 hr on ice. Uranyl acetate treated samples were briefly washed three times in distilled water, dehydrated using a series of increasing ethanol concentration and finally embedded in epoxy resin (Agar 100 kit, Plano, Germany) and polymerized for 48 hr at 70°C. An Ultracut E microtome (Leica Microsystems, Germany) equipped with a 35° diamond knife (Diatome, Switzerland) was used to obtain ultrathin sections (70–75 nm) of the specimen. Sections were transferred to 1% formvar-coated (w/v in water-free chloroform) copper slot grids (ATHENE copper slot grids, 3.05 mm Ø, 1 mm x 2 mm; Plano, Germany) and subsequently stained with uranyl acetate replacement solution (UAR-EMS) (Science Services, Germany) and Reynold’s lead citrate. The specimens were investigated at 80 kV with a JEM1011 transmission electron microscope (JEOL, Germany) and micrographs acquired at 10,000-x magnification using a Gatan Orius 1200A camera (Gatan, Germany, using the Digital Micrograph software package). Serial 3D reconstructions of ultrathin sections were generated with the program Reconstruct (Fiala, 2005).

### High-pressure freezing/freeze-substitution (HPF/FS) and electron tomography

High-pressure freezing, freeze-substitution followed by electron tomography were essentially performed as described previously (Vogl et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2015a). After freeze-substitution and embedding in epoxy resin (Agar 100 kit, Plano, Germany), 250 nm semithin sections for electron tomography were obtained on an Ultracut E ultramicrotome (Leica Microsystems, Germany) with a 35° diamond knife (Diatome, Switzerland). Sections were placed on 1% formvar-coated (w/v in water-free chloroform) copper 100 mesh grids (ATHENE, Plano, Germany, 3.05 mm Ø) and post-stained with UAR-EMS (Science Services, Germany) and Reynold’s lead citrate.

For electron tomography, 10 nm gold particles (British Bio Cell/Plano, Germany) were applied to both sides of the stained grids. Single tilt series at 12,000-x magnification, mainly from −60 to +60° (if only fewer angles were possible, the tomograms were only accepted for quantification if the quality was sufficient) were acquired with an 1° increment at a JEM2100 (JEOL, Germany)) transmission electron microscope at 200 kV using the Serial-EM software (Mastronarde, 2005). The tomograms were generated using the IMOD package etomo and models were generated using 3dmod (Kremer et al., 1996).

### Data analysis

Live-imaging and IHC-patch-clamp data were analyzed using custom programs in Igor Pro 6.3 (Wavemetrics, Portland, OR, USA; Source Code 2). For analysis of IV-curves, the evoked Ca2+-current was averaged from 5 to 10 ms after the start of the depolarization. The total Ca2+-charge was estimated by taking the integral of the leak-subtracted current during the depolarization step. For most protocols, ΔCm was estimated as the difference between the mean of Cm 400 ms after and before the depolarization (the initial 60 ms after the end of depolarization were skipped). For paired pulse experiments, the calculation of the mean of Cm before and after the depolarization was limited to the time remaining in the inter pulse interval after skipping (the initial 30 ms after the end of depolarization were skipped).

ΔF images were generated by subtracting the fluorescence intensity inside the cell at the resting state (F0, an average of 10 frames) from the one at the depolarized state (an average of 6 frames during voltage ramp protocol). ΔF was calculated as the average of a 3 × 3 pixel square placed in the region showing the greatest intensity increase within the fluorescence hotspot. Maximal ΔF (ΔFmax) was the average of 5 ΔF values obtained between −17 and +8 mV during the voltage ramp (around the peak Ca2+-influx). Only AZs presenting a ΔFmax greater than the mean of the fluorescence intensity plus two standard deviations at rest were considered for further analysis. For analysis of the voltage dependence of synaptic Ca2+-signals, raw traces were fitted to the following

$$
F(V)=F_{0}+\frac{f_{v}⋅(V_{r}−V)}{1+e^{\frac{(V_{h}−V)}{k}}}
$$

where $f_{v}$ is the fluorescence-voltage-relationship ΔF/ΔV obtained by linear fitting to the FV-curve in the range of 3 to 23 mV, $V_{r}$ the reversal potential of 65.6 mV, and $V$ the command voltage, in order to obtain $V_{h}$, the voltage of half-maximal activation, and $k$, the slope factor. The spatial extent of the synaptic Ca2+-signals was estimated by fitting of a 2D Gaussian function to the fluorescent hotspot using a genetic fit algorithm (Sanchez del Rio and Pareschi, 2001) to obtain the full width at half maximum in the long and short axis. For each spot, the calculations were made at those confocal sections where the intensity of the spot was strongest.

Activation time constants of Ca2+-currents at differing potentials were obtained by fitting to the first 5 ms of the current traces the following equation:

$$
f(t)=y_{0}+A\times(1−e^{(\frac{−x}{\tau})})^{2}
$$

Confocal and STED immunofluorescence images were analyzed and z-projected with Fiji software and further analyzed using Igor Pro. For synapse counting, co-localized pre- and postsynaptic immunofluorescent spots were counted manually. The spatial extent of the line-shaped Ca2+-channel clusters was estimated by fitting a 2D Gaussian function to the individual clusters in 2D STED images to obtain the full width at half maximum in the long and short axis. The areas of the PSD were calculated by the following formula: area = π x (Long Axis/2) (Short Axis/2). The semi-quantitative immunofluorescence analysis of the proteinaceous Ca2+-buffers was performed by calculating the mean immunofluorescence intensity of a volume (40 (X) x 40 (Y) x 4 (Z) voxels or 2.8 × 2.8 × 2 µm) below the nucleus and above the synapses. This and the count and intensity of the CtBP2 immunofluorescent spots have been analyzed in Imaris 7.6.5 with custom Matlab routines (Source Code 4).

For extracellular SGN recordings, PSTHs were calculated as average firing rates across 200 presentations of 50 ms or 500 ms tone bursts presented at 0.1 s/0.2 s or 2 s intervals, resp. (PSTH at 10/5 Hz and 0.5 Hz) at Cf, 30 dB above the threshold and binned at a width of 2 ms. Peak rate was determined as the largest bin of the PSTH in a time window 3–11 ms after stimulus onset. Adapted rate was averaged in a window spanning 35–45 ms or 405–415 ms after stimulus onset (for PSTH at 5 Hz and 0.5 Hz, respectively). Rate level functions were acquired using 50 ms tone bursts presented at Cf and at 5 Hz. 25 repetitions for each stimulus intensity (5 dB steps) were recorded. Maximal steepness was calculated as the maximal increase in spike rate between two consecutive 5 dB increment steps. Dynamic range was calculated by using sigmoidal fits in the rate level functions as described in and measuring the range of sound pressure between 10% and 90% of maximal firing rate. For amplitude modulation analysis, synchronization index was calculated as described by (Goldberg and Brown, 1969). Synchronization index estimation was only considered valid when at least 15 spikes occurred in a 3 s time window and the Rayleigh statistic was below 13.8.

For analysis of forward masking experiments, spike counts in a 10 ms interval starting from responses of both masker and probe onset were determined and presented as the ratio of probe and masker responses for at least 25 repetitions for every masker-probe interval from each unit. Exponential fitting to the plots of each individual SGN approximated the recovery kinetics.

Quantitative analysis of electron microscopy data was performed with ImageJ for conventional embedded samples and with IMOD for HPF/FS tomograms. According to the presence of ribbon-occupied and ribbonless synapses, we considered the following analysis criteria:

For ribbon-occupied synapses, membrane-proximal synaptic vesicles (MP-SVs, within a distance of ≤25 nm from the AZ membrane and ≤80 nm from the presynaptic density) and ribbon-associated synaptic vesicles (RA-SVs, first layer around the ribbon with a maximum distance of 80 nm from the vesicle membrane to the ribbon) were counted (Figure 2J, random sections analysis according to Strenzke et al., 2016 and Figure 3G for tomograms according to 2D-random section analysis criteria). The tomogram analysis parameters were further modified, as used in Jung et al., 2015a. Here, the MP-SVs were defined as vesicles with ≤50 nm from the AZ membrane and with the shortest distance from the vesicle membrane to the presynaptic density of ≤100 nm, excluding RA-SVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). For random sections, SV diameters were calculated by the averaged measurements of the horizontal and vertical axis. The ribbon size was measured in height and width, taking the longest axis of the ribbon excluding the PD, and the edges of the synaptic ribbon were traced manually using ImageJ. The length of the PD was measured along the AZ membrane (Figure 2J).

For ribbonless synapses, a presynaptic density-associated synaptic vesicle (PDA-SVs) pool was defined considering all clustered vesicles ≤80 nm around the PD that did not fulfill the criteria of a MP-SV (see above, also Figure 2J for random sections). The MP-SV pool, as well as the SV diameter and PD length, were analyzed as for the ribbon-occupied synapses. For tomograms, the PDA-SV pool was defined as the SVs in the first layer ≤ 80 nm to the PD, excluding the MP-SVs. The MP-SV pool criteria are the same as described in the previous paragraph (Figure 3G, according to 2D-random section and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, according to Jung et al., 2015a). For tomograms, the according pools were further distinguished into tethered and non-tethered vesicles (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). All vesicles were annotated using a spherical ‘scattered object’ at its maximum projection in the tomogram, encompassing the outer leaflet of the vesicles. The vesicle radii were determined automatically (Helmprobst et al., 2015) with the program ‘imodinfo option -p’ of the IMOD software package (Kremer et al., 1996).

### Release site model of RRP release and replenishment

The coding of sound onset differs among the various SGNs in time due to different durations of the traveling wave, synaptic delays and conduction times. To obtain an average PSTH for modeling that is not smeared out due to such differences between units, the individual PSTHs were aligned beforehand by shifting their timing relative to each other. Onset detection was based on a change in spike statistics. For spontaneous activity, the 99.5 percentile of spike counts was determined. Next, the time at which response rises to twice this percentile was found. This is certainly a point within the sound response. Finally going back from this point, a drop back baseline activity, that is below the percentile was detected and used as onset time. Aligned PSTH from all units were averaged. This averaged PSTH from the forward masking data were fit with a model waveform using a genetic fit algorithm implemented in IGOR Pro (Wavemetrics, Lake Oswego, OR, USA). The purpose of the model is to give insight into the dynamics of SV cycling at the average IHC AZ. More specifically, the notion of Ca2+-nanodomain-like control of RRP exocytosis (Brandt et al., 2005; Graydon et al., 2011; Pangršič et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2014), as well as the limited MP-SVs at the AZ (see Figures 2 and 3) motivates the notion of a limited, quasi-fixed number of available vesicular release sites or slots, Nslot,(Frank et al., 2010; Wong et al., 2014) that constitute the RRP. Each of these sites can be either empty or occupied by a release ready SV (whereby all filled slots constitute the ‘standing’ RRP) and at each time point, a release ready SV will fuse with a certain probability described by the fusion rate constant kfus. Its value depends on the sound pressure level in a relation we assume to be linear within the dynamic range of the synapse/fiber. While the sound pressure level rises from silence to saturation kfus increases from kfus, spont to kfus,stim. The refilling of empty sites is described by a refill rate constant krefill, which also depends on the sound intensity (krefill, spont to krefill,stim).

The state of the release site was described by:

$$
\frac{dN_{slot}^{filled}(t)}{dt}=k_{refill}(t)N_{slot}−N_{slot}^{filled}(t)(k_{fus}(t)+k_{refill}(t))
$$

Although this equation is formulated for SV fusion rates, a scaling factor f can be used to account for the fraction of fusion events that cannot successfully trigger an action potential (AP) despite sufficient neural excitability for example because of the too small size of the elicited excitatory post synaptic current. This factor effectively operates as if the number of release sites was scaled down. The scaled equation then gives a rate R of potentially supra-threshold EPSCs as the product of the number of occupied release sites, the fusion rate constant and the scaling factor f:

$$
R(t)=k_{fus}(t).f.N_{slot}^{filled}(t)
$$

The stationary solutions of Equation 3 together with Equation 4 determine steady state occupancy and steady state event rates:

$$
N_{solt}^{filled}|_{stradystate}^{condition}=\frac{K_{refill}^{condition}}{K_{fusion}^{condition}+K_{refill}^{condition}}.N_{solt}
$$



$$
R|_{stradystate}^{condition}=\frac{K_{fusion}^{condition}.f.K_{refill}^{condition}}{K_{fusion}^{condition}+K_{refill}^{condition}}.N_{solt}
$$

In this equation, ‘condition’ is either silence or saturating sound pressure level.

In order to connect the postsynaptic event rate of potentially supra-threshold EPSCs to the actual AP rate, refractoriness is considered as a combination of an absolute refractory period tabs, during which the probability of an EPSC to trigger an AP is zero, with a relative refractory period during which this trigger probability returns to one with an exponential time course characterized by τrel (Berry and Meister, 1998). This description of refractoriness can be applied to the ‘driving’ EPSC rate R by means of a delayed differential equation. The equation is motivated by the concept of three possible states of the SGN: ‘absolute refractory’, ‘relative refractory’ or ‘available’ (fully excitable). At any point, the probability that the SGN turns from ‘available’ to ‘refractory’ is proportional to the rate R(t). The return back to ‘available’ happens ‘delayed’ by tabs and with a probability that is proportional to 1/τrel.

$$
\frac{df_{avail}(t)}{dt}=\frac{f_{relref}(t)}{\tau_{rel}}−f_{avail}(t).f.R(t)\frac{df_{relref}(t)}{dt}=f_{avail}(t−t_{abs}).f.R(t−t_{abs})−\frac{f_{relref}(t)}{\tau_{rel}}
$$

Together with Equation 6 the stationary solution of this description of refractoriness connects the observable steady state rates during silence and stimulation to the rate constants krefill und kfusion:

$$
AP_Rate|_{stradystate}^{condition}=\frac{K_{fusion}^{condition}.f.K_{refill}^{condition}}{K_{fusion}^{condition}+K_{refill}^{condition}}.N_{solt}.\frac{1}{1+R|_{stradystate}^{condition}(t_{abs}+\tau_{rel})}
$$

To go beyond the description of steady state event rates and to use the model for a parameterized description of the actual time course of experimentally observed PSTHs acquired during forward masking (Figure 11E), it is necessary to define the relation between the applied stimulus and the fusion and refill rate constants. For the experimental data presented here, the stimulus level was increased from silence to 30 dB above fiber threshold within a 4 ms ramp having a quarter of a sin² shape. It was assumed that kfusion and krefill follow the stimulus increase simultaneously. The ordinary differential and delayed differential equations above were combined into a fit function. PSTHs (one masker followed by one probe) were averaged per genotype for each masker probe interval (4, 16, 64 and 256 ms) and were fitted in parallel with one parameter set. During experiments, trials were acquired in immediate succession without gaps. Therefore, the model implements cyclic boundary conditions for the occupancy of the slots. This model only captures the short term processes, assuming that a set of experiments, for example forward masking trials quickly lead to a steady state. Slow adapting processes were not explicitly modeled. The observed drop of the apparent number of available slots in the forward masking experiments was described here as a change in the number of slots from Nslots to a reduced capacity N’slots and for a given spiral ganglion neuron that was tested with tone bursts and forward masking, the ratio Nslots/N’slots could be estimated from the change in rates (see Results).

### Statistical analysis

The data were analyzed using Matlab (Mathworks), Excel, Igor Pro 6 (Wavemetrics), Origin 9.0 (Microcal Software), and GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software). Averages were expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (S.E.M.). For every dataset, the standard deviation (S.D.), number of replicates (n) and animals (N) were indicated. For Figure 7, nmin corresponds to the minimum number of cells included in the analysis of each depolarization potential given that the number of cells for each potential differs. In order to compare two samples, data sets were tested for normal distribution (Jarque-Bera test, D’Agostino and Pearson omnibus normality test or the Shapiro-Wilk test) and equality of variances (F-test), followed by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test, or, when data were not normally distributed and/or variance was unequal between samples, the unpaired two-tailed Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test was used. Cumulative distributions in Figure 9A were statistically compared using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. The ROUT method (Q = 0.1%) from GraphPad Prism was used to identify definitive outliers for Figure 7H.

For multiple comparisons, statistical significance was calculated by using one-way ANOVA test (two-way ANOVA in the case of ABR thresholds) followed by Tukey’s test for normally distributed data or Kruskal-Wallis (K-W) test followed by non-parametric multiple comparisons test (NPMC) for non-normally distributed data.

For SV diameter quantifications in random sections, a custom-written routine using Java Statistical Classes library (JSC) (Bertie, 2002) was utilized for statistical analysis (Source code 5). Due to the tied ranks of SV diameter measurements obtained for random sections, their S.E.M. was used as a tolerance value for the usage of Kruskal-Wallis test as suggested by Bertie et al. in JSC library (Bertie, 2002), where two values were treated as equal if their difference was ≤ S.E.M.. Thank you for submitting your article "The synaptic ribbon is critical for sound encoding at high rates and with temporal precision" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Andrew King as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

This decision was reached by discussion between the Reviewing Editor and the reviewers, and the Reviewing Editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission. Both reviewers highlighted the fact that your study explores a major issue, the role of the ribbon in IHC synaptic exocytosis, and that the article is based on a large, high-quality data set and is very well written.

However, there is a major issue that needs to be resolved. Both reviewers felt that it was necessary to clarify the discordance between some of the results reported in the two jointly submitted manuscripts, which explore the same mouse Ribeye KO/KO mutant. These discrepancies include, in particular, the modifications to the Ca2+-currents of the KO mice. The authors of the two manuscripts are therefore requested to work together to iron out these discrepancies.

The work performed on the zebrafish Ribeye mutants also requires additional attention (Lv et al., Cell Reports 2016). This work shows that frameshift mutations in the gene encoding Ribeye lead to "ghost ribbons" in zebrafish neuromast hair cells. What evidence is there to suggest that the situation is different in the KO mouse mutant studied? This point should be addressed with care. The results obtained in the zebrafish mutants are generally insufficiently taken into account and discussed in this article, and should be expanded.

Reviewer #1:

There are at least 2-3 major discrepancies between this and the companion paper, despite the fact that both investigate the same RIBEYE KO mouse. First, there were no differences observed in ABR threshold as were reported in the companion paper. Second, there are significant differences in the biophysics of the Ca2+-current (i.e. V-half activation) between KO and WT mice that are not reported in the companion paper. This discrepancy could be due to the large variability in the data presented in both studies, possibly indicating some issues with IHC viability. Third, the DCm measurements were found to be significantly different between -43 and -53 mV in this paper, while the companion study only showed a difference at -40 mV and not at -45 mV.

Reviewer #2:

1) What was the average value of Rs for the data in Figure 5? If the Rs =20 MΩ and I(Ca) = 150 pA then the voltage-clamp error is 3 mV. So I am a bit skeptical by the small shifts reported to about 5 mV, although Figure 6 gives me more confidence in the conclusions. The labels in Figure 5 and 6E and other Figures are much too small, so please increase the font size in the figures to the largest amount possible. Consider that the figures will be shrunk in size later on.

2) Figure 7 shows that strong stimulation reveals no difference between RBE-KO-mice and WT-mice for IHC exocytosis, but Figure 8 shows that ABR wave I amplitude is much smaller at 80 dB (a strong stimulus). This seems like a contradiction. What is the explanation? Perhaps a lack of highly synchronous EPSPs that trigger spikes in a phase-locked manner (variance in FSL; Figure 9F) and an increase in spike failures due to smaller evoked EPSPs in the RBE-KO-mice? Some more discussion and explanation would be helpful.

3) Figure 11D shows a highly significant difference in the vector strength. The authors should also mention here that larger EPSCs are better phase-locked than smaller EPSCs (see Li et al., Neuron, 2014; see their Figure 8). So one would also expect lower vector strength and reduced phase locking in the KO mice to be related to a smaller frequency of large EPSCs. Indeed, this is what the companion paper of Becker et al. (Ricci group) seems to find. So it seems appropriate to mention this previous paper while discussing Figure 11D.

4) Show the Bassoon-KO mice data also on Figure 9H and 9I (using a different color or symbol).

5) In contradiction to this paper, the companion paper of Becker et al. found significant changes in the ABR thresholds and no change in the Ca2+-current properties. This should be discussed briefly. Maybe the methods are different or the number of animals studied? German mice and American mice should behave the same, right?

claims.evidence: Quantitative membrane capacitance measurements

claims.claim: Trains of 20 step-depolarizations do not reveal impaired exocytosis in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
claims.source: Moreover, trains of 20 step-depolarizations to −17 mV of 20 ms pulse duration did not reveal impaired exocytosis in RBEKO/KO IHCs, even when the inter-stimulus interval time was as short as 160 ms (Figure 7D; n = 11 cells, N = 5 for RBEWT/WT and n = 13 cells, N = 8 for RBEKO/KO).
claims.evidence: Membrane capacitance measurements during repetitive stimulation

claims.claim: RRP recovery from partial depletion is not altered in RBEKO/KO IHCs when probed with maximal Ca2+-influx.
claims.source: We further explored RRP recovery from partial depletion using a paired-pulse protocol (two strong 20 ms depolarizations to −14 mV separated by 50, 110, 260 and 510 ms inter-pulse intervals; Figure 7E,F). RRP recovery, estimated as the ΔCm ratio of the second and the first pulse, was not altered in RBEKO/KO IHCs at least when probing RRP exocytosis with maximal Ca2+-influx from a hyperpolarized resting potential (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Paired-pulse membrane capacitance measurements

claims.claim: Exocytosis for stronger depolarizations (e.g., to -39 mV) is not significantly different between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT IHCs.
claims.source: In agreement with the results obtained at maximal Ca2+-influx, we did not find significant differences in ΔCm for stronger depolarizations (e.g. pulses to −39 mV elicited an average ΔCm of 20.67 ± 7.46 fF, S.D. = 23.58 fF, nmin = 10 IHCs, N = 9 for RBEKO/KO vs. 24.12 ± 4.04 fF, S.D. = 13.98 fF, nmin = 10 IHCs, N = 9 for RBEWT/WT; p=0.20; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
claims.evidence: Membrane capacitance measurements at different depolarization potentials with statistical comparison

claims.claim: Exocytosis for weaker depolarizations in the range of physiological receptor potentials is subtly but significantly reduced in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
claims.source: However, for weaker depolarizations in the range of physiological receptor potentials (Russell and Sellick, 1983), we observed a subtle but significant reduction in exocytosis for RBEKO/KO IHCs (Figure 7H, p=0.0115, p=0.0295 and p=0.1321 for −45, –43 and −41 mV; without definitive outliers as determined by Graphpad Prism: p=0.0017, p=0.0042 and p=0.0489, respectively; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test for all).
claims.evidence: Membrane capacitance measurements at different depolarization potentials with statistical comparison and citation to previous characterization of physiological receptor potentials

claims.claim: The amplitude of ABR wave I is significantly reduced in RBEKO/KO mice.
claims.source: First, we recorded auditory brainstem responses (ABR) and found a significant reduction in the amplitude of wave I that reflects the SGN compound action potential (1.14 ± 0.13 µV, S.D. = 0.38 µV, N = 10 for RBEKO/KO vs. 3.30 ± 0.51 µV, S.D. = 1.54 µV, N = 10 for RBEWT/WT, p=0.0007, NPMC test).
claims.evidence: ABR recordings with statistical comparison

claims.claim: Reduced ABR wave I amplitude indicates less synchronous SGN activation in the absence of synaptic ribbons.
claims.source: This indicates less synchronous SGN activation in the absence of synaptic ribbons (Figure 8A,B).
claims.evidence: Interpretation of ABR wave I amplitude reduction based on understanding of what wave I represents

claims.claim: Subsequent ABR waves (II, IV and V) are normal in amplitude in RBEKO/KO mice.
claims.source: The subsequent ABR waves (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) were normal in amplitude (waves II, IV and V, while wave III was reduced)
claims.evidence: ABR recordings showing normal amplitudes for specific waves

claims.claim: ABR wave III is reduced in RBEKO/KO mice.
claims.source: The subsequent ABR waves (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) were normal in amplitude (waves II, IV and V, while wave III was reduced)
claims.evidence: ABR recordings showing reduced amplitude for wave III

claims.claim: Normal amplitudes of subsequent ABR waves indicate a degree of central auditory compensation for the sound encoding deficit.
claims.source: indicating a degree of central auditory compensation for the sound encoding deficit, for example via coincidence detection of converging SGN input in the cochlear nucleus (Joris et al., 1994; Strenzke et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Interpretation of normal subsequent ABR waves with citations to previous work on central auditory processing

claims.claim: Cochlear amplification is intact in RBEKO/KO mice.
claims.source: Cochlear amplification, probed by recordings of distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAE, Figure 8D), was intact in RBEKO/KO mice.
claims.evidence: DPOAE recordings showing normal cochlear amplification

claims.claim: RBEWT/KO mice show no significant changes in ABR wave I amplitudes and ABR thresholds.
claims.source: Additionally, RBEWT/KO mice showed no significant changes in ABR wave I amplitudes and ABR thresholds (Figure 8)
claims.evidence: ABR recordings from heterozygous mice showing no significant differences

claims.claim: There is an increased abundance of SGNs with low spontaneous firing rates in RBEKO/KO mice.
claims.source: We first assessed the spontaneous firing activity and found an increased abundance of SGNs with low spontaneous firing rates in RBEKO/KO mice (72% with rates < 10 Hz, n = 43 SGNs, N = 9 vs. 50% in RBEWT/WT, n = 40 SGNs, N = 8; p=0.0267, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: Extracellular recordings from single SGNs with statistical comparison

claims.claim: Frequency tuning is intact in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: Frequency tuning was intact in RBEKO/KO SGNs (Figure 9B): the sharpness of tuning expressed by the Q10dB (width of tuning curve 10 dB above threshold at the characteristic frequency (Cf) normalized by Cf) was comparable (mean: 9.28 ± 1.01, S.D. = 6.32 and median: 7.41 for RBEKO/KO SGNs, n = 39 SGNs, N = 9 vs. mean: 12.50 ± 1.98, S.D. = 11.91 and median: 8.36 for RBEWT/WT SGNs, n = 36 SGNs, N = 9; p=0.28, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
claims.evidence: Analysis of frequency tuning curves from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison

claims.claim: The sound threshold at characteristic frequency is significantly elevated by almost 20 dB in RBEKO/KO mice.
claims.source: However, the sound threshold at Cf was significantly elevated by almost 20 dB in RBEKO/KO mice (35.60 ± 3.45 dB SPL, S.D. = 22.66 dB SPL for RBEKO/KO SGNs, n = 43 SGNs, N = 9 vs. 16.05 ± 2.47 dB SPL, S.D. = 15.42 dB SPL for RBEWT/WT SGNs, n = 39 SGNs, N = 9, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: Analysis of sound thresholds from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison

claims.claim: The threshold increase in RBEKO/KO SGNs seems unlikely to result from a functional cochlear deficit upstream of the IHCs given normal frequency tuning and DPOAE.
claims.source: Given the normal frequency tuning and DPOAE, this threshold increase seems unlikely to result from a putative functional cochlear deficit upstream of the IHCs.
claims.evidence: Inference based on combination of normal frequency tuning and DPOAE with elevated thresholds

claims.claim: Peak firing rate at sound onset is reduced in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: We observed reduced spike rates of SGNs from RBEKO/KO mice (Figure 9D,E) both at sound onset (p=0.0001, n = 39 SGNs, N = 8 in RBEKO/KO and n = 38 SGNs, N = 9 in RBEWT/WT, t-test)
claims.evidence: Analysis of PSTH from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison

claims.claim: Adapted firing rate is reduced in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: We observed reduced spike rates of SGNs from RBEKO/KO mice (Figure 9D,E) both at sound onset (p=0.0001, n = 39 SGNs, N = 8 in RBEKO/KO and n = 38 SGNs, N = 9 in RBEWT/WT, t-test) and after short-term adaptation (p=0.0023, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
claims.evidence: Analysis of PSTH from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison

claims.claim: The mean apparent adaptation time constant is significantly slowed in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: The mean apparent adaptation time constant reported by single-exponential fitting were significantly slowed in RBEKO/KO SGNs (9.83 ± 0.50 ms, S.D. = 2.85 ms, median: 10.46 ms, n = 32 SGNs, N = 8) as compared to RBEWT/WT SGNs (8.71 ± 0.50 ms, S.D. = 3.05 ms, median: 8.73 ms, n = 37 SGNs, N = 9, p=0.033, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
claims.evidence: Exponential fitting to PSTH data with statistical comparison

claims.claim: First spike latency is prolonged in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: As expected for the reduced peak firing rate, we found prolonged first spike latency which also showed greater temporal jitter (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: Analysis of first spike timing from single SGN recordings

claims.claim: First spike latency shows greater temporal jitter in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: As expected for the reduced peak firing rate, we found prolonged first spike latency which also showed greater temporal jitter (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: Analysis of first spike timing variability from single SGN recordings

claims.claim: The reduced peak firing rate together with increased first spike latency jitter likely explain the reduction in ABR wave I amplitude.
claims.source: The reduced peak firing rate together with increased first spike latency jitter likely explain the reduction in ABR wave I amplitude.
claims.evidence: Inference connecting single SGN firing properties to ABR wave I amplitude

claims.claim: The firing of putative AVCN neurons is better preserved than SGN firing in RBEKO/KO mice.
claims.source: The firing of putative AVCN neurons was better preserved: putative bushy cells showed normal sound driven rates and chopper cells only a mild reduction in peak rate (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: Extracellular recordings from cochlear nucleus neurons

claims.claim: The spike rate increase with sound pressure level is not significantly altered in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: These 'rate-level functions' (Figure 11A) indicated that the spike rate increase with the sound pressure level (p=0.068, n = 24 SGNs, N = 8 in RBEKO/KO and n = 19 SGNs, N = 7 in RBEWT/WT, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test, Figure 11—figure supplement 1A)
claims.evidence: Analysis of rate-level functions from single SGN recordings with statistical comparison showing no significant difference

claims.claim: The dynamic range of sound coding is not significantly altered in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: and the dynamic range of sound coding (sound pressure level for which the spike rate changes from 10–90%, Figure 11—figure supplement 1B, p=0.3044, t-test) were not significantly altered.
claims.evidence: Analysis of dynamic range from rate-level functions with statistical comparison showing no significant difference

claims.claim: The maximal firing rate of RBEKO/KO SGNs is reduced when probed with transposed tones.
claims.source: We then used transposed tones (Cf at 500 Hz modulation frequency) in order to probe for the temporal fidelity and reliability of firing in RBEKO/KO SGNs in the steady state (Figure 11D). These experiments corroborated the reduced maximal firing rate of RBEKO/KO SGNs (n = 22 SGNs, N = 7 in RBEKO/KO and n = 15 SGNs, N = 6 in RBEWT/WT, p<0.0001, t-test)
claims.evidence: Analysis of responses to transposed tones with statistical comparison

claims.claim: The temporal precision of sound coding is impaired in the steady state in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: and indicated that the temporal precision of sound coding is impaired also in the steady state (reduced Synchronization Index: p=0.0043, t-test).
claims.evidence: Analysis of synchronization to transposed tones with statistical comparison

claims.claim: The time constant of recovery from forward masking is prolonged in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
claims.source: The time constant of recovery was prolonged in RBEKO/KO SGNs (90.80 ± 8.66 ms, S.D. = 45.00 ms, n = 27 SGNs, N = 8 vs. 33.53 ± 5.74 ms, S.D. = 28.11 ms, in RBEWT/WT SGNs, n = 24 SGNs, N = 7, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test)
claims.evidence: Exponential fitting to forward masking recovery data with statistical comparison

claims.claim: Prolonged recovery from forward masking indicates slowed RRP replenishment in the absence of the ribbon.
claims.source: indicating slowed RRP replenishment in the absence of the ribbon.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of prolonged recovery time constant based on understanding of forward masking paradigm

claims.claim: Biophysical modeling suggests that the total number of release sites (RRP) is only slightly reduced at ribbonless synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs.
claims.source: Taken together the fits from forward masking and tone bursts suggest that the total number of release sites (RRP) was only slightly reduced at ribbonless synapses of RBEKO/KO IHCs.
claims.evidence: Results from biophysical modeling of SGN responses

claims.claim: A strong firing response at sound onset requires longer recovery in RBEKO/KO, indicating more efficient SV replenishment in the presence of ribbons.
claims.source: However, a strong firing response at sound onset, that is release of a large standing RRP, required longer recovery indicating more efficient SV replenishment in the presence of ribbons, which is reflected in the larger refilling rate constants estimated by the model of RBEWT/WT synapses.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of modeling results and experimental observations regarding recovery times

claims.claim: RIBEYE is required for ribbon formation in mammalian IHCs.
claims.source: Our work confirms the central role of RIBEYE for forming synaptic ribbons (Schmitz et al., 2000; Magupalli et al., 2008; Maxeiner et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Summary statement with citations to previous work establishing RIBEYE's role in ribbon formation

claims.claim: The synaptic ribbon is important for sound encoding at high rates and with temporal precision at IHC synapses.
claims.source: In summary, we demonstrate that the synaptic ribbon is important for sound encoding at high rates and with temporal precision at IHC synapses.
claims.evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings throughout the study

claims.claim: The ribbon has a role in organizing the topography of the IHC active zone.
claims.source: Combining assessments of the molecular anatomy from electron and fluorescence microscopy with cell and systems physiology, we revealed a role for the synaptic ribbon in organizing the topography of the IHC AZ, in Ca2+-channel regulation and in vesicle replenishment.
claims.evidence: Summary statement based on morphological findings showing multi-AZ organization in RBEKO/KO

claims.claim: The ribbon has a role in Ca2+-channel regulation.
claims.source: Combining assessments of the molecular anatomy from electron and fluorescence microscopy with cell and systems physiology, we revealed a role for the synaptic ribbon in organizing the topography of the IHC AZ, in Ca2+-channel regulation and in vesicle replenishment.
claims.evidence: Summary statement based on findings of altered Ca2+-channel voltage-dependence and spatial organization

claims.claim: The ribbon has a role in vesicle replenishment.
claims.source: Combining assessments of the molecular anatomy from electron and fluorescence microscopy with cell and systems physiology, we revealed a role for the synaptic ribbon in organizing the topography of the IHC AZ, in Ca2+-channel regulation and in vesicle replenishment.
claims.evidence: Summary statement based on findings of slowed recovery from adaptation and reduced vesicle pools

claims.claim: The multi-AZ morphology of RBEKO/KO IHC synapses reflects a compensatory effort rather than developmental delay.
claims.source: While we cannot rule out some sort of developmental delay of RIBEYE-deficient IHCs, we suspect that the morphological transformation into a multi-AZ morphology reflects a compensatory effort.
claims.evidence: Interpretation based on multiple lines of evidence including persistence in older animals and mature synaptic features

claims.claim: The loss of synaptic Ca2+-channels from bassoon-deficient ribbonless IHC synapses indicates a role of bassoon in promoting Ca2+-channel tethering at the AZ.
claims.source: Therefore, the loss of synaptic Ca2+-channels from the bassoon-deficient ribbonless IHC synapses, indicates a role of bassoon in promoting Ca2+-channel tethering at the AZ likely via interaction with RIM-binding protein (Davydova et al., 2014), which was previously shown to interact with CaV1.3 Ca2+-channels (Hibino et al., 2002) and is required for establishing a normal Ca2+-channel complement of the IHC AZ (Krinner et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Inference based on comparison with bassoon mutants and citations to previous work on protein interactions

claims.claim: The depolarized Vh-shift of synaptic Ca2+-influx is relevant for hair cell transmission.
claims.source: A small, but significant reduction of exocytosis for weak depolarizations in RBEKO/KO IHCs (Figure 7, seen also in the accompanying paper by Becker et al.) suggests that the Vh shift is relevant for hair cell transmission (see also below).
claims.evidence: Inference connecting the observed Vh shift to functional consequences in exocytosis

claims.claim: Some features of the IHC ribbon-type AZ can be replaced by a ribbonless multi-AZ morphology.
claims.source: In fact, our study of IHCs, unlike the situation for bipolar cell retinal ribbons (Maxeiner et al., 2016), suggests that some features of the IHC ribbon-type AZ can be very well replaced by a ribbonless multi-AZ morphology: the synaptic complement of Ca2+-channels and SVs, as well as exocytic ΔCm elicited by strong depolarizations, were similar.
claims.evidence: Summary interpretation based on findings of normal Ca2+-channel numbers and exocytosis for strong stimuli, with citation to contrasting findings in retina

claims.claim: The study likely underestimated the role of the ribbon due to substantial compensation.
claims.source: Therefore, we likely underestimated the role of the ribbon in sound encoding in our present study.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on observation of compensatory multi-AZ morphology

claims.claim: Two mechanisms with likely additive effects explain impaired sound encoding despite unaltered exocytic ΔCm: the depolarized shift of synaptic Ca2+-channels and reduced SV-replenishment.
claims.source: We propose two mechanisms with likely additive effects to explain this surprising finding: i) the small depolarized shift of synaptic Ca2+-channels might contribute the lower spontaneous and evoked firing rates as well as higher sound thresholds of SGNs and ii) the reduced SV-replenishment might not suffice to balance the rate of consumption leading to a smaller standing RRP in vivo, while the arrest of exocytosis in the voltage-clamped IHCs for tens of seconds likely enables complete filling of the release sites (max. standing RRP).
claims.evidence: Proposed mechanistic explanation integrating multiple experimental findings

results.result: RIBEYE is required for ribbon formation in mammalian IHCs, as RBEKO/KO mice completely lack synaptic ribbons as demonstrated by electron microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C73 are strongly supported by transmission electron microscopy data from random sections showing complete absence of ribbons in RBEKO/KO IHCs, consistent with previous work establishing RIBEYE's central role in ribbon formation. The evidence is direct, quantitative, and corroborated by multiple imaging modalities.

results.result: Ribbonless RBEKO/KO IHC synapses maintain normal synapse number and retain key presynaptic scaffold proteins (bassoon, RIM2) but lose piccolino.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence showing unchanged PSD-95 spot counts (C2), persistent bassoon and RIM2 at synapses (C3-C4), and absence of piccolino (C5). The data are internally consistent and include appropriate statistical comparisons with adequate sample sizes.

results.result: Postsynaptic densities are significantly enlarged in RBEKO/KO IHCs compared to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C13 are supported by quantitative analysis using both immunofluorescence (C6: p<0.0001) and electron microscopy (C13: p=0.01 vs. RBEWT/KO). The convergent evidence from two independent methods strengthens the conclusion of PSD enlargement.

results.result: RBEKO/KO IHC synapses display multiple presynaptic densities per active zone, a phenotype that persists in older animals and is confirmed by serial 3D reconstruction and electron tomography.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 and C18 are well-supported by electron microscopy showing multiple PDs per contact in random sections, serial reconstructions (average 1.92 PDs), and tomography. The persistence at 6 weeks and 8 months (C10) argues against developmental delay, though this inference could be strengthened with additional developmental timepoints.

results.result: The lateral extent of individual presynaptic densities is comparable between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT synapses.
results.evaluation: Claim C12 is supported by quantitative electron microscopy measurements showing no significant difference (p=0.92, NPMC test) with adequate sample sizes (n=108 PDs per genotype, N=2 animals). The statistical test is appropriate for the data.

results.result: RBEKO/KO IHCs show reduced membrane-proximal and PD-associated synaptic vesicles compared to wild-type, with altered vesicle pool distributions but preserved tethering fractions.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 and C19-C23 are supported by quantitative electron microscopy (random sections and tomography) with appropriate statistical tests. The reduction in MP-SVs (C14, C19) and PDA-SVs (C15, C22) is statistically significant, while tethering fractions remain unchanged (C20, C23). The finding of increased multiple-tethered MP-SVs (C21) is interesting but mechanistically unexplained.

results.result: Ribbons in heterozygous RBEWT/KO IHCs are significantly smaller in all dimensions compared to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claim C8 is supported by quantitative electron microscopy showing statistically significant reductions in ribbon height, width, and area (all p<0.0001) with adequate sample sizes (n>100 ribbons per genotype). This demonstrates a hypomorphic phenotype in heterozygotes.

results.result: CaV1.3 Ca2+-channels remain clustered at RBEKO/KO synapses but are reorganized into multiple smaller, rounder clusters per synaptic contact.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by confocal and STED super-resolution immunofluorescence showing persistent CaV1.3 clustering (C24) but altered spatial organization with >70% of synapses showing multiple clusters (C25-C26) and significantly increased average cluster number (C27: p<0.0001). The data are consistent with the multi-AZ morphology observed by EM.

results.result: The amplitude and activation kinetics of whole-cell Ca2+-currents are unaltered in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C29, and C32 are supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings showing no significant differences in Ca2+-current amplitude (p=0.62), activation kinetics, or voltage-sensitivity (p=0.67). Sample sizes are adequate (n=21 cells per genotype) and statistical tests appropriate.

results.result: Ca2+-channel inactivation is slightly faster and the voltage-dependence of activation is shifted to more depolarized potentials in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C30 and C31 are supported by patch-clamp data showing statistically significant but small changes: faster inactivation (p=0.017) and 2 mV depolarizing shift in Vh (p=0.017). While statistically significant, the biological significance of these small changes requires functional validation, which is partially provided by claims C46 and C80.

results.result: Maximal amplitudes and voltage-sensitivity of synaptic Ca2+-influx are comparable between RBEKO/KO and RBEWT/WT IHCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C33 and C35 are supported by confocal Ca2+-imaging showing no significant differences in maximal ΔF/F0 (p=0.20) or slope factor (p=0.42). This indicates that the total Ca2+-channel complement at synapses is preserved despite the multi-AZ reorganization.

results.result: The voltage for half-maximal activation of synaptic Ca2+-influx is shifted by 5 mV to more depolarized potentials in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 is supported by confocal Ca2+-imaging showing a statistically significant 5 mV depolarizing shift (p=0.0029). This larger shift at individual synapses compared to whole-cell measurements (C31: 2 mV) is explained by the contribution of extrasynaptic channels to whole-cell currents, strengthening the interpretation.

results.result: The spatial extent of synaptic Ca2+-signals is significantly greater at RBEKO/KO active zones.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by quantitative analysis of Ca2+-imaging showing significantly increased FWHM in both axes (p=0.00016 and p=0.0029). This is consistent with the multi-cluster organization of CaV1.3 channels observed by STED microscopy (C25-C27) and argues against altered Ca2+-buffering (C37).

results.result: Immunofluorescence intensities of major Ca2+-binding proteins are unchanged in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by semi-quantitative immunofluorescence showing no significant differences for parvalbumin-α, calretinin, and calbindin-28k (all p>0.05). This controls for the possibility that altered Ca2+-buffering contributes to the broader spatial spread of Ca2+-signals (C36).

results.result: Exocytosis in response to strong depolarizations is unaltered in RBEKO/KO IHCs, including fast RRP release, sustained exocytosis, repetitive stimulation, and RRP recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C45 are supported by perforated-patch membrane capacitance measurements showing no significant differences in ΔCm for strong depolarizations across multiple protocols. The data are comprehensive and include appropriate controls. However, this surprising result contrasts with the in vivo phenotype and is partially explained by claims C46 and C83.

results.result: Exocytosis for weak depolarizations in the physiological range is subtly but significantly reduced in RBEKO/KO IHCs.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by membrane capacitance measurements showing statistically significant reductions at -45 and -43 mV (p=0.0115, p=0.0295), with stronger significance after outlier removal. This is consistent with the depolarized Vh shift (C31, C34) and provides a mechanistic link to the in vivo phenotype. The citation to physiological receptor potential ranges strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: ABR wave I amplitude is significantly reduced in RBEKO/KO mice, indicating less synchronous SGN activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C47 and C48 are supported by ABR recordings showing a statistically significant reduction in wave I amplitude (p=0.0007). The interpretation that this reflects reduced synchrony (C48) is reasonable given that wave I represents the compound action potential, though direct evidence of synchrony would require single-unit recordings.

results.result: Subsequent ABR waves show normal amplitudes (II, IV, V) except for wave III, suggesting central auditory compensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by ABR recordings showing preserved amplitudes for most central waves. The interpretation of central compensation (C51) is reasonable and supported by citations to previous work on coincidence detection, though alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

results.result: Cochlear amplification is intact in RBEKO/KO mice as measured by DPOAE.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 is supported by DPOAE recordings showing normal cochlear amplification. This is important for ruling out outer hair cell dysfunction as a contributor to the auditory phenotype and supports the interpretation that deficits arise from IHC synaptic dysfunction.

results.result: Heterozygous RBEWT/KO mice show no significant changes in ABR wave I amplitudes or thresholds.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is supported by ABR recordings showing no significant differences in heterozygotes. This indicates that the morphological changes observed in heterozygous IHCs (C8) do not translate to measurable functional deficits at the systems level, at least as assessed by ABR.

results.result: RBEKO/KO mice show an increased abundance of SGNs with low spontaneous firing rates.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by extracellular single-unit recordings showing a statistically significant shift in the distribution of spontaneous rates (p=0.0267, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test). This is consistent with the depolarized Vh shift reducing spontaneous transmitter release.

results.result: Frequency tuning is intact in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by analysis of frequency tuning curves showing comparable Q10dB values (p=0.28). This indicates that the basic cochlear mechanics and frequency selectivity are preserved, consistent with normal DPOAE (C52).

results.result: Sound thresholds at characteristic frequency are significantly elevated by ~20 dB in RBEKO/KO SGNs, likely due to IHC synaptic dysfunction rather than upstream cochlear deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C56 and C57 are supported by single-unit recordings showing statistically significant threshold elevation (p<0.0001). The inference that this is not due to upstream cochlear deficits (C57) is reasonable given normal frequency tuning (C55) and DPOAE (C52), though the logic is inferential rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: RBEKO/KO SGNs show reduced peak and adapted firing rates with slowed adaptation kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by PSTH analysis showing statistically significant reductions in both peak (p=0.0001) and adapted rates (p=0.0023), with slowed adaptation time constants (p=0.033). The data are consistent across multiple stimulation paradigms and support impaired vesicle replenishment.

results.result: First spike latency is prolonged with greater temporal jitter in RBEKO/KO SGNs, likely explaining the reduced ABR wave I amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by analysis of first spike timing showing increased latency and jitter. The inference connecting these findings to ABR wave I amplitude (C63) is reasonable, as increased jitter would reduce synchrony of the compound action potential, though this is inferential rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Firing of putative AVCN neurons is better preserved than SGN firing in RBEKO/KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by extracellular recordings showing normal rates in bushy cells and only mild reduction in chopper cells. This is consistent with central compensation (C51) and suggests that convergence of SGN inputs can partially overcome the peripheral deficit.

results.result: Rate-level functions and dynamic range of sound coding are not significantly altered in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C65 and C66 are supported by analysis of rate-level functions showing no significant differences in slope (p=0.068) or dynamic range (p=0.3044). This indicates that intensity coding is relatively preserved once threshold is exceeded, consistent with the finding that strong depolarizations produce normal exocytosis (C38-C45).

results.result: Maximal firing rate and temporal precision of sound coding are impaired in the steady state in RBEKO/KO SGNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C67 and C68 are supported by analysis of responses to transposed tones showing reduced maximal firing rate (p<0.0001) and synchronization index (p=0.0043). This demonstrates that the deficit persists during sustained stimulation and affects temporal coding.

results.result: Recovery from forward masking is significantly prolonged in RBEKO/KO SGNs, indicating slowed RRP replenishment.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C70 are supported by forward masking experiments showing a nearly 3-fold increase in recovery time constant (p<0.0001). The interpretation that this reflects slowed RRP replenishment (C70) is reasonable given the forward masking paradigm, though alternative explanations (e.g., altered adaptation mechanisms) are not fully excluded.

results.result: Biophysical modeling suggests that the total number of release sites is only slightly reduced at ribbonless synapses, but efficient replenishment requires ribbons for maintaining a large standing RRP.
results.evaluation: Claims C71 and C72 are supported by biophysical modeling of SGN responses to multiple stimulation paradigms. The modeling provides a mechanistic framework for reconciling the mild ex vivo exocytosis phenotype (C38-C45) with the pronounced in vivo deficit. However, the model makes several assumptions that are not fully validated.

results.result: The synaptic ribbon is important for sound encoding at high rates and with temporal precision, with roles in organizing AZ topography, Ca2+-channel regulation, and vesicle replenishment.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 represent the main conclusions of the study and are supported by the convergent evidence from morphology (multi-AZ organization), Ca2+-channel function (depolarized Vh shift, altered spatial organization), vesicle pools (reduced MP-SVs and PDA-SVs), and in vivo function (reduced firing rates, slowed recovery). The evidence is comprehensive and internally consistent.

results.result: The multi-AZ morphology of RBEKO/KO IHC synapses reflects a compensatory effort rather than developmental delay.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is based on several lines of evidence (persistence in older animals, mature synaptic features) but remains speculative. While the authors provide reasonable arguments against developmental delay, definitive proof would require developmental time-course studies or conditional knockout experiments. The claim is explicitly presented as speculation ('we suspect').

results.result: The loss of synaptic Ca2+-channels in bassoon-deficient synapses indicates a role for bassoon in Ca2+-channel tethering at the AZ.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is an inference based on comparison with bassoon mutants and is supported by citations to previous work on protein interactions. The logic is sound: since RBEKO/KO synapses retain Ca2+-channels but bassoon mutants lose them, bassoon must have a ribbon-independent role in Ca2+-channel tethering. However, this is inferential rather than directly demonstrated in this study.

results.result: The depolarized Vh-shift of synaptic Ca2+-influx is functionally relevant for hair cell transmission.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by the observation of reduced exocytosis for weak depolarizations (C46), which is consistent with the Vh shift. The inference connecting the Vh shift to functional consequences is reasonable, though the relative contributions of the Vh shift versus other mechanisms (e.g., reduced vesicle replenishment) are not fully disentangled.

results.result: Some features of the IHC ribbon-type AZ can be replaced by a ribbonless multi-AZ morphology, including Ca2+-channel and SV complement and exocytosis for strong stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by the findings of normal Ca2+-channel numbers (C28, C33), normal exocytosis for strong depolarizations (C38-C45), and the multi-AZ morphology (C9-C11). The comparison with retinal bipolar cells strengthens the interpretation. However, the claim that features are 'very well replaced' may overstate the case given the clear in vivo deficits.

results.result: The study likely underestimated the role of the ribbon due to substantial compensation.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is speculative and based on the observation of compensatory multi-AZ morphology. While this is a reasonable interpretation, it is difficult to assess the extent of compensation without additional experiments (e.g., acute ribbon disruption). The claim is explicitly presented as speculation.

results.result: Impaired sound encoding despite unaltered exocytic ΔCm is explained by two additive mechanisms: depolarized shift of Ca2+-channels and reduced SV-replenishment that is insufficient in vivo but masked ex vivo.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 represents a mechanistic synthesis of multiple findings and is supported by the depolarized Vh shift (C31, C34), reduced exocytosis for weak depolarizations (C46), slowed recovery from adaptation (C69), and modeling results (C71-C72). The proposed mechanisms are reasonable and internally consistent, though the relative contributions of each mechanism are not quantitatively determined. The explanation for why ex vivo measurements don't fully capture the in vivo deficit is plausible but somewhat speculative.
